check.x: Professionalism
Introduces self, explains what is being done in plain language, stays calm with the anxious, intoxicated patient, and gives short closed-loop instructions to the nurse.
Uses standard precautions for a bleeding patient: gloves, gown and eye protection.
History
Takes a focused AMPLE history once the primary survey is under way:

kids.x: Allergies: penicillin, and clarifies the reaction (childhood itchy rash only, no swelling or breathing trouble)
Medications: salbutamol and recent ibuprofen (bleeding risk, asthma), no anticoagulants
Past history: mild asthma, previous nasal fracture, no operations
Last meal about 3 hours ago and about 6 beers, relevant to any procedure or sedation
Events: the mechanism, the time of injury, no loss of consciousness, and nasal blockage on both sides

check.x: Asks about tetanus immunisation: childhood course completed, last dose in Year 10, booster status unknown.
Examination: primary survey and nose

Works through A, B, C, D and E in order, treats problems as found and reassesses after each intervention. Controlling the open neck wound at once (for example, directing the nurse to press on it while the airway is assessed) is correct, not out of order.
Airway with cervical spine control:

kids.x: Asks him to speak, inspects the mouth for blood, clots and teeth, and looks for stridor, neck swelling and surgical emphysema
Applies manual in-line stabilisation or a collar because of the mechanism, alcohol and distracting injury

check.x: Breathing: checks RR and SpO2, examines the chest (trachea, expansion, percussion, auscultation) and gives high-flow oxygen.
Recognises the right neck laceration as a possible external jugular vein injury and explains the danger:

kids.x: The wound over sternocleidomastoid lies in the line of the external jugular vein, and the platysma is breached
The investing fascia holds the cut vein open, so breathing in while upright can suck air in (venous air embolism); notes the sucking noise

check.x: Immediately occludes the wound and protects against air embolism:

kids.x: Direct pressure with a gloved finger or gauze straight away, then an occlusive dressing
Lies him flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation, not left sitting upright with the wound open
Calls early for senior help: ED consultant and the trauma or surgical team

check.x: Circulation: assesses perfusion and prepares for bleeding:

kids.x: HR, BP, capillary refill and skin temperature (108, 114/72, 3 seconds, cool), and looks for other bleeding
Two large-bore cannulae with bloods: FBC, coagulation studies, group and crossmatch, venous gas with lactate

check.x: Disability: GCS, pupils, limb neurology and a bedside glucose (GCS 15, pupils equal and reactive, BGL 5.6).
Exposure: fully exposes, log-rolls with spinal precautions, measures core temperature (35.2 °C), removes wet clothing and starts active warming (warm blankets, forced-air warmer, warmed fluids).
Examines the nose with correct technique:

kids.x: Inspects and palpates the external nose, notes epistaxis or clear rhinorrhoea (CSF leak), and checks midface stability, eye movements and dental occlusion
Uses a headlight and nasal speculum, with suction to clear clots and topical decongestant as needed

check.x: Identifies a bilateral nasal septal haematoma: smooth, red-purple, fluctuant septal swelling that does not shrink with decongestant and is soft to a cotton bud, unlike a firm deviated septum.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: the yellow zone temperature on arrival (35.2 °C) calls for a clinical review, here the senior-led trauma assessment; after occlusion, positioning and oxygen he is haemodynamically stable (HR 108 to 96, BP 122/76) with no further bleeding or air entrainment, but still hypothermic at 35.6 °C, so active warming continues.
States the trauma deadly triad and links it to the results:

kids.x: Hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis, each worsening the others and increasing mortality
Here: hypothermia on arrival, a mild lactic acidosis (pH 7.31, lactate 2.4, base excess -3) and normal coagulation so far

check.x: States that a normal haemoglobin (131 g/L) early after injury does not exclude significant blood loss, and repeats it.

Interprets the CT: external jugular vein injury without arterial, airway or oesophageal injury; no cervical spine fracture; displaced nasal fractures with a bilateral septal haematoma, confirming the clinical diagnosis.
Management
Explains the diagnosis to Daniel in plain words: a collection of blood between the cartilage of the middle of the nose and its lining.
Explains the risks of leaving it untreated: septal abscess, cartilage necrosis, saddle nose deformity and septal perforation.
Explains the treatment: drainage today by the ENT team or a senior, then packing or splinting to stop it re-collecting, and antibiotics.
Answers "can this wait?" with empathy: it cannot wait for the swelling to settle and must be drained today; checks understanding.

States what to do if venous air embolism develops (sudden breathlessness, chest tightness, hypoxia, hypotension, mill-wheel murmur): occlude the wound, lie him flat or head-down, left lateral tilt only as a log-roll with spinal precautions, 100% oxygen and senior help.

Continues to prevent the deadly triad: active warming, limits crystalloid, and activates the massive transfusion protocol with early balanced blood products and considers tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury if bleeding recurs or shock develops.

Chooses an antibiotic for the septal haematoma active against Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci per eTG, considering the allergy: a cephalosporin may be reasonable for a remote, non-severe rash; avoids penicillins if the reaction was immediate or severe.
Analgesia: regular paracetamol with titrated IV opioid; avoids NSAIDs for now because of bleeding risk and asthma.

Tetanus: a dirty, glass-contaminated wound with the last dose more than 5 years ago needs a tetanus-containing booster (dTpa); checks the Australian Immunisation Register; tetanus immunoglobulin is not needed if at least 3 doses are documented.
Disposition: ENT for drainage today, the trauma or surgical team for wound exploration and repair, admission for observation, and factual documentation of the assault.
Safety netting

Tells Daniel and the nurses what to report at once: sudden breathlessness or chest pain, bleeding or swelling at the neck, a blocked nose returning after drainage, fever, or worsening nose pain. After discharge he calls 000 for breathlessness or neck bleeding and returns to ED for these symptoms.

Arranges follow-up: ENT review for pack removal and to check for re-collection, nasal fracture review at about 1 week for possible reduction, wound review and suture removal, tetanus recorded, a brief alcohol intervention and support after the assault (social work, and police if he wishes), and a GP letter.

desc: This station involves a trauma primary survey with immediate management of a neck wound over the external jugular vein, a focused AMPLE history and a nasal examination, then interpreting the reassessment, blood gas, bloods and CT report, and managing and explaining a nasal septal haematoma with safety netting.
explain:
Summary

This man has two life- or tissue-threatening problems hidden behind an apparently minor assault. The first is a right neck wound over the external jugular vein, with an air entrainment risk. The second is a bilateral nasal septal haematoma that needs same-day drainage.

Primary survey (ABCDE)

Airway with cervical spine control comes first, then Breathing, Circulation (with haemorrhage control), Disability and Exposure. Call for help early and reassess after every intervention. Alcohol and a distracting injury mean the cervical spine cannot be cleared clinically, so in-line stabilisation continues until imaging and senior review allow it to come off under the local trauma protocol.

External jugular vein laceration

The external jugular vein runs deep to platysma and pierces the investing layer of deep cervical fascia above the clavicle, where its wall is bound to the fascia, so a cut vein is held open instead of collapsing. When the patient is upright, venous pressure at the neck is low or negative and inspiration can draw air into the circulation, causing venous air embolism. Features are sudden dyspnoea, chest tightness, hypoxia, hypotension and a mill-wheel murmur.

  • Immediately occlude the wound with direct finger or gauze pressure, then apply an occlusive dressing.

  • Lay the patient flat or head-down (Trendelenburg) with in-line stabilisation so that venous pressure at the neck is raised. Use head-down tilt with caution if there is a head injury.

  • If air embolism is suspected, a left lateral tilt may be used, but in a trauma patient it must be done as a log-roll with spinal precautions.

  • Get urgent senior help and give high-flow oxygen. A wound that breaches the platysma needs CT angiography of the neck once stable, and surgical exploration and repair.

Interpreting the results

After occlusion, positioning, oxygen and warming he is stable, which is the expected response. He is still hypothermic. The venous gas shows a mild lactic acidosis, and the coagulation results are normal so far. A normal haemoglobin soon after injury does not exclude significant blood loss, because haemoglobin falls only as fluid shifts or is given, so it is repeated. The CT angiogram confirms an external jugular vein injury without arterial, airway or oesophageal injury, the cervical spine shows no fracture, and the facial CT shows displaced nasal fractures with septal thickening that matches the clinical septal haematoma.

Trauma deadly triad

Hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis each worsen the others and increase mortality. Prevent them by controlling haemorrhage, warming the patient actively (remove wet clothes, warm blankets, forced-air warmer, warmed fluids), limiting crystalloid and giving early balanced blood products through the massive transfusion protocol if bleeding is significant. Consider tranexamic acid within 3 hours if bleeding is significant. Follow lactate, base excess and coagulation results.

AMPLE

Allergies, Medications, Past medical history (and pregnancy where applicable), Last meal, and Events and environment. Here the allergy history is only useful if the reaction is clarified, because a remote non-severe rash is handled differently from anaphylaxis. Recent ibuprofen adds to bleeding risk, and alcohol and the last meal matter for any procedure.

Nasal septal haematoma

Blood collects between the septal cartilage and its perichondrium and cuts off the cartilage's blood supply. The presentation is nasal obstruction (often bilateral) after trauma with a smooth, red-purple, fluctuant septal swelling that does not shrink with decongestant. Untreated, it risks septal abscess, cartilage necrosis, saddle nose deformity and septal perforation. Treatment is urgent drainage as soon as it is diagnosed, usually with packing or splinting to prevent re-accumulation, plus antibiotics. Do not wait for swelling to settle.

Other management

  • Antibiotics follow eTG and local guidance, with the penicillin reaction type clarified.

  • Analgesia is paracetamol with titrated opioid, avoiding NSAIDs for now.

  • For a tetanus-prone wound with the last dose more than 5 years ago, give a tetanus-containing booster (dTpa). Tetanus immunoglobulin is not needed with at least 3 documented doses.

  • Complete a secondary survey, arrange ENT and surgical review, admit for observation, and document the assault factually.

Safety netting and follow-up

He and the nursing staff need to know the warning signs: sudden breathlessness or chest pain (air embolism), bleeding or swelling at the neck, a blocked nose returning, fever or worsening nose pain (re-collection or abscess). Follow-up covers ENT review for pack removal and re-collection, nasal fracture review at about a week for possible reduction, wound review and suture removal, the tetanus dose recorded on the Australian Immunisation Register, a brief alcohol intervention, and support after the assault.
focus: Trauma primary survey in the ED: neck and nasal injuries
guide:
In Part 1, the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings as the candidate works through the primary survey and examines the nose. The primary survey comes first; mark the History items whenever the AMPLE history is taken. If the candidate leaves him upright with the wound open, say that the sucking noise is still heard with each breath in. In Part 2, hand over the reassessment, blood gas and bloods, and the CT report, then ask the questions in order, reading out Daniel's question for the third.

A high-performing candidate works in ABCDE order, recognises the neck wound as a possible external jugular vein injury and occludes it at once with pressure and an occlusive dressing. They lie him flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation, call for senior help early, and start active warming. They take a rapid AMPLE history, clarify the penicillin reaction, and examine the nose with a light, speculum and suction to identify a septal haematoma. In Part 2 they link the hypothermia and mild lactic acidosis to the deadly triad, note that an early normal haemoglobin is reassuring only up to a point, read the CT correctly, explain the risks of the septal haematoma and the need for drainage today, and cover air embolism, antibiotics, analgesia, tetanus, disposition and follow-up.

A borderline candidate leaves the patient sitting upright with the neck wound open, or does not explain why it is dangerous. They omit cervical spine control or warming, cannot name the deadly triad, or take a vague AMPLE history. They do not use a speculum, miss the septal haematoma or offer reassurance and discharge, and omit the tetanus, antibiotic and follow-up plans.
patient:
Role: You are Daniel Hartnett, a 32-year-old electrician. You are anxious and a bit drunk, sitting upright on the trolley holding a wad of gauze to your nose. Answer in short sentences. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings as the candidate works through the primary survey and examines your nose.

Opening line: "Mate, my nose is killing me and I can't breathe through it. Is my neck bad?"

During the primary survey: do what the candidate asks: speak when asked, keep your head still if they hold it or put on a collar, lie flat if asked. If the candidate leaves you sitting up with the neck wound open, the examiner tells them that a sucking noise is still heard at the wound with each breath in.

History (give only when asked):

  • Events: about 45 minutes before arrival you were punched in the nose outside a hotel, then a bottle was smashed and swiped across the right side of your neck. You did not lose consciousness, did not hit your head on the ground and remember everything. Your nose is blocked on both sides and throbs. The neck cut does not hurt much, but it was bleeding a lot.
  • Allergies: penicillin. You had an itchy rash as a child and your mother told you not to take it. There was no swelling and no trouble breathing. Say this only if asked what the reaction was.
  • Medications: a salbutamol puffer when needed. You take ibuprofen occasionally for gym aches and took two tablets this morning. No blood thinners.
  • Past history: mild asthma. You broke your nose playing football 10 years ago and had no surgery. No other operations.
  • Tetanus: you had your childhood vaccinations and your last tetanus needle was in Year 10 at school. You do not know whether you have had a booster since.
  • Last meal: a burger about 3 hours ago. About 6 beers over the evening. No other drugs.
  • Other symptoms: no headache, no vomiting, no blurred or double vision, no clear fluid running from the nose, no neck weakness, numbness or tingling. No pain anywhere else.
  • Social: you live with your partner and work as an electrician.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think your nose is broken again and the neck just needs a few stitches. You are worried about missing work. You want to get patched up and go home to sleep.

Question to ask once (in Part 2, after the candidate explains what is wrong with your nose): "I just want to go home and sleep. Can this wait until the swelling goes down?" If the candidate uses jargon, say "What does that mean?"
points: ABCDE: Airway (with cervical spine control), Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure. Work in order, treat as you go and call for help early.
AMPLE: Allergies, Medications, Past history (and pregnancy), Last meal, Events and environment. Clarify the allergy reaction type because it changes the antibiotic.
Trauma deadly triad: hypothermia, coagulopathy and acidosis. Prevent them with haemorrhage control, warming and early balanced blood products.

A superficial neck wound over the external jugular vein can entrain air because the investing fascia holds the cut vein open. Occlude it at once with pressure and an occlusive dressing, position flat or head-down with in-line stabilisation and get senior help.
In trauma, a left lateral tilt for suspected air embolism must be done as a log-roll with spinal precautions.
A septal haematoma risks septal abscess, cartilage necrosis, saddle nose and septal perforation. Treat with urgent drainage, packing or splinting, and antibiotics.
refs: Royal Australasian College of Surgeons. Early Management of Severe Trauma (EMST) course, based on the American College of Surgeons Advanced Trauma Life Support Student Course Manual, 10th edition (2018).
National Blood Authority. Patient Blood Management Guidelines: Module 1 Critical Bleeding/Massive Transfusion. Canberra: NBA; 2011.
Australian Immunisation Handbook. Tetanus chapter, including tetanus-prone wound management (Australian Government Department of Health and Aged Care).
Therapeutic Guidelines. Antibiotic. Melbourne: Therapeutic Guidelines Limited; current version.
stem: You are the emergency registrar. Mr Daniel Hartnett, a 32-year-old man, has arrived by ambulance after being punched in the face and cut on the right side of the neck with a broken glass bottle during a fight outside a hotel. Paramedics report that their dressing came off during transfer. He is now sitting upright on the trolley with the neck wound exposed and a blood-stained shirt. A nurse is with you and can carry out any instructions you give. Monitoring is being attached.
tasks: Perform a primary survey (ABCDE), telling the examiner what you are examining and starting immediate management as you go. Then take a focused AMPLE history and examine the nose (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you his reassessment, blood gas and blood results, and the CT report. Interpret them, then outline your management approach, explaining the nasal diagnosis and its treatment to the patient, and your safety netting (5 minutes).
title: Assault with neck laceration and nasal injury

part2.lead: Here is his reassessment after your initial management, his blood gas and blood results, and the CT report.

handover.label: Reassessment 20 minutes later
handover.result: Lying flat with in-line stabilisation, occlusive dressing on the neck wound, oxygen 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask and forced-air warming. The dressing is dry with no further bleeding or sucking noise. CRT 2 seconds (3 seconds and cool peripheries on arrival). GCS 15. Heart sounds normal with no murmur.
handover.model:
• Read: on arrival HR 108, BP 114/72, RR 20 and SpO2 96% on air are in the white zone, but the temperature of 35.2 °C is in the yellow zone, with cool peripheries and a CRT of 3 seconds. After occlusion, lying flat, oxygen and warming, HR falls to 96, BP rises to 122/76 and SpO2 is 99%; the temperature is still yellow at 35.4 °C at 23:30 and reaches 35.6 °C at 23:40, just inside the white zone.
  • Meaning: on arrival he was compensating for blood loss (tachycardia and cool peripheries with a normal BP; a white zone HR does not exclude it) and he has responded to haemorrhage control. The yellow zone temperature called for a clinical review, which the senior-led trauma assessment provides, and he is still hypothermic below 36 °C although the chart is now white.
  • Changes: keep warming actively and keep him flat with the wound occluded, observations every 15 minutes, and escalate to the trauma team again for a rising HR, falling BP, fresh bleeding or sudden breathlessness.

rows.note: Arrival in resus: sitting upright, neck wound oozing
Wound occluded; lying flat with in-line stabilisation; forced-air warmer on
Reassessment: dressing dry, no sucking noise

handover.label: Venous blood gas and bloods (on arrival)
handover.model:
• Read: venous pH 7.31 with base excess -3 and lactate 2.4 is a mild lactic acidosis; a venous pCO2 of 45 is normal. Hb 131 g/L is at the lower limit; platelets, INR, APTT, fibrinogen and ionised calcium are normal; WCC 13.6 is a stress response. Blood is crossmatched (O positive).
  • Meaning: two parts of the deadly triad are present, hypothermia on arrival and acidosis from hypoperfusion, and coagulopathy is not, yet. An early normal Hb does not exclude significant blood loss, because it falls only as fluid shifts or is given.
  • Changes: keep warming, avoid large volumes of crystalloid, and repeat the gas, Hb and coagulation. If bleeding recurs, give blood early through the massive transfusion protocol and consider tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury.

rows.v: O positive, antibody screen negative, 2 units crossmatched

handover.label: CT report
handover.result:
Examination: CT angiogram of the neck (arterial phase, after IV contrast), with reformats of the cervical spine and facial bones.

Clinical details: 32-year-old man. Glass laceration to the right side of the neck breaching platysma, with venous bleeding and a sucking noise on inspiration before it was occluded. Punched in the face: nasal deformity and bilateral septal swelling. Intoxicated.

Findings:

  • Neck soft tissues: 5 cm laceration over the right sternocleidomastoid with gas in the wound track, and a small (2 cm) haematoma deep to platysma around the right external jugular vein, which is discontinuous at the wound, in keeping with a laceration. No active contrast extravasation. No gas in the internal jugular or subclavian veins or the imaged superior vena cava.
  • Arteries: common, internal and external carotid and vertebral arteries opacify normally, with no dissection, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm, occlusion or extravasation.
  • Internal jugular veins: intact and patent.
  • Aerodigestive tract: larynx, trachea and oesophagus intact. No gas in the deep neck spaces, retropharyngeal space or mediastinum.
  • Cervical spine: normal alignment. No fracture. Prevertebral soft tissues normal.
  • Facial bones: displaced fractures of both nasal bones with deviation of the nasal pyramid to the left. Smooth soft tissue thickening on both sides of the anterior nasal septum, in keeping with a septal haematoma. No naso-orbito-ethmoid, orbital, maxillary, zygomatic or mandibular fracture.
  • Lung apices: clear. No pneumothorax.

Conclusion: right external jugular vein laceration with a small haematoma; no arterial, airway, oesophageal or cervical spine injury. Displaced nasal bone fractures with a bilateral nasal septal haematoma.
handover.model:
• Read: the right external jugular vein is cut beneath the wound with a small haematoma; the carotid and vertebral arteries, internal jugular vein, larynx, trachea and oesophagus are intact and there is no gas in the deep veins. The cervical spine is normal. Both nasal bones are fractured and displaced, with soft tissue thickening on both sides of the septum.
  • Meaning: the neck injury is confined to the external jugular vein, which explains the venous bleeding and the risk of air entrainment; the septal thickening confirms the bilateral septal haematoma found on examination.
  • Changes: the trauma or surgical team explores and repairs or ligates the vein, with air embolism precautions until then; ENT drains the septal haematoma today. The cervical collar can come off under the local trauma protocol with senior review, and the nasal fractures are reviewed for reduction at about 1 week.

ask: What do his reassessment, blood gas and bloods show? How do they relate to the trauma deadly triad?
What does the CT show, what is your diagnosis for the nose, and what must you still watch for with the neck wound?
Explain the nasal problem and its treatment to Daniel. He says: "I just want to go home and sleep. Can this wait until the swelling goes down?"
What is the rest of your management: antibiotics, analgesia, tetanus, disposition and who you involve?
What safety netting and follow-up does he need?
